utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, "successfully" is not what I read in the statement. Or am I mistaken? I'm looking at 27?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour. There is probably slight --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Lukic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- difference in the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please switch on your microphone, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. I think it might be a slight difference in the translation because this word does appear in B/C/S version. It's in the middle of the first line of paragraph 27, "uspjesno."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Uspjesno" means "successfully"?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I was reading from B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then the -- it may not be that important to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it -- if I may, Your Honour, I think it does matter because I would say that the -- eventually the successful defence of that ground lay with the Bosnian forces. What I was doing was conducting a delaying operation to buy time. That was all. To keep the ground until it could be held by those who had to defend it. So from that -- to that extent it was successful. I think, Mr. Lukic, if my memory serves me correctly, you asked me if I was fighting on the same side as the Bosnians. You didn't ask me if I was waging war on the Serbs, the two being slightly different.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But at the same time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we understand that you were successful in saving the town by keeping the attack off for a while and Muslims -- allowing the Muslims to take over your positions, and it was not successful, however, in terms of pushing back the attacking Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that's -- I think that's a good summary, Your Honour. I believed that that ground was vital to the safety of the town and therefore the civilians in it, that I had to hold it; if I couldn't hold, it must be held by those who would defend the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now paragraph 29 of your statement, please, the very same statement that we see before us. "With the OP line gone and few convoys coming in, our usefulness to the Muslims had disappeared. They became very restrictive ..." When did that happen and what did that mean, that they became very restrictive towards you? What do we have then, the situation that we saw in that document?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but which document? You've shown me quite a --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where it says --

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: You've shown me a lot of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay, sorry. The document, if we can have it -- let's -- first tell us --

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Sorry, was this the 12th Division in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, indeed. We're now talking, I think, about middle to late July, and the fighting which grew up around the enclave in the aftermath of the 28th of May had subsided, but I was not able to re-occupy the OP line because the TEZ had, to all intents and purposes, disappeared and the lines had moved. And therefore, there was - as I now know - discussion going on about whether we should stay or not and the British government later announced that we would be brought out. And at this point, the Bosnian forces began to try to restrict our movements, both locally around the town and in and out of the enclave. Although once the resupply convoys had restarted, both for ourselves and for UNHCR, they did not obstruct those because it would not have been in their interest to do so. But life certainly became -- and it had been difficult enough before, it became very much more difficult when both sides were trying to close us down. I guess that's impartiality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to ask you something about paragraph 30 that you changed today. Paragraph 30. You speak about your withdrawal from the enclave. First I'd like to ask you when it was that you received this message, to withdraw from the enclave of Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: The British government had issued instructions that we should withdraw - and I'm sorry, I'm going to have to look up the date if you'll forgive me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we know what you are consulting at this moment, your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. It's a book called "White Dragon," which was compiled from my diaries and other people's diaries at the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, whenever you consult anything else than your own statement, which approval was given that you would have it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we'd like to know what you're consulting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm afraid I can't find the date but I believe it was sometime --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you're only looking for the date itself, I do understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was -- the British government's decision I think was sometime in early August, around about a month before our six-month tour of duty was due to end. So that was the stated intention that we would -- we would withdraw and not be replaced. And that was communicated, as far as I understand, to both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question, please, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: According to this statement, you said to us in paragraph 30, that in the morning you received news of the NATO air-strikes. Do you remember when that happened in the morning when you heard the news of NATO air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But wasn't this part of the correction, Mr. Lukic? The witness said, at least as far as I remember: We didn't hear about the NATO air-strikes but we heard about a shelling incident which perhaps likely or could have resulted in NATO air-strikes. That's how the witness corrected his statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In my question only the -- what matters is the timing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At what time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- he received the message.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. At what time then -- the question now is: At what time did you receive the information about the shelling incident which you considered to be at risk to trigger air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be exactly sure, I would have to consult the war diary, which I don't have. But my recollection was that it was late morning, around about 11.00, something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can't assist you. Mr. Lukic, next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How long did it take you to organise your unit for withdrawal and when did you leave the Gorazde enclave?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: The withdrawal had been going on for at least two weeks. Following the meeting with General Mladic, we had removed as many personnel vehicles and heavy equipment as was not immediately required. We had distributed a good deal of furniture and food to the -- to the hospitals on both sides -- on both the Serb and the Bosnian side. So by the time we got to this date which you're referring about -- referring to, there were only -- I think only 80 soldiers in total left in Gorazde in the -- in the force with just sufficient vehicles to lift them and only their personal weapons and ammunition. So with -- given that in mind -- given that, it took me only an hour to -- to organise the final move.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know, did anyone inform you, that the decision to bomb the Serbian positions was adopted on the London Conference on the 21st of July of 1995? This is at least according to General Smith's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I have seen the written message delivered by Air Marshal Ratan [phoen] and others to the Serb side in Belgrade after the London Conference, which warned the Serb side that if they attacked Gorazde and put the lives of UN peacekeepers there at risk, then they would be attacked with -- and I think the exact words were "substantial air power," which would be delivered with enough resource to stop them pushing forward their attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of the proposal of Western powers that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be divided 49 Republika Srpska and 51 the remainder of Bosnia-Herzegovina which is today the Federation? Were you aware of these efforts of the Western Alliance at the time when you arrived in Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I was a lieutenant-colonel commanding a battalion and not really in the -- in the councils of the great. What I had -- what I did know about was the Vance-Owen Plan, which had been accepted by the Serb side, as I recall, but not by the other parties. But that, as far as I was aware, was the only deal that was on the table at the moment. I was not sufficiently senior, I think, to be aware of any other proposals at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Air Marshal Ratan, who you just mentioned, issued an ultimatum relating to air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I think as I just said in answer to your question, I've seen the written warning. And it was a warning, I would say, not an ultimatum. It did not say that we are going to attack you. It said that if you do so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, again, remain seated. Mr. Lukic, my -- the patience of the Chamber is coming to an end.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I check with the "White Dragon" for a moment because I think it may have the text of the Ratan warning in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, before I -- Mr. Stojanovic nods that he has no problems. Usually this is decided once the parties have expressed themselves. You may have a look at the text. Mr. Mladic, low voice. Mr. Lukic, please, it's now the third or fourth time this morning that I have to intervene. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My client insists that I ask you the following: Do you know anything about the meeting at which Air Marshal Ratan issued a warning, as you put it, to General Mladic? And do you know who else attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I've only seen the text, the written text, of the warning. I don't know Air Marshal Ratan. I might have met him once subsequently. I'm not sure who else was there. The text of the message was sent to me, there being no internet in those days, by fax. And I believe I still have somewhere the original document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're referring to a meeting, that meeting being --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The meeting being with Air Marshal Ratan. I think it was with the president of Yugoslavia and in Beograd.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this same paragraph, number 30, you say: "We were warned that we were facing a serious attack by BH 'renegades,' who were redoubling their efforts to foil our retreat." Under such circumstances, did any specific and direct attacks occur against your forces by the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Yes, we had been attacked two days before by the Bosnian forces. I think this -- there are two possible reasons. One was to try to steal weapons, food, ammunition, equipment. The other was that the local Bosnian military commanders did not understand that the British government's desire to withdraw its troops was a measure to -- for protection and that the -- the protection that the United Nations could afford to Gorazde would then be undertaken by air power rather than by what was left of a battalion. They thought that the withdrawal of the battalion meant that they were going to be abandoned, so I think that their view was that if the Serbs could take hostages to achieve an end, then so would they. So I think it was entirely possible that they were playing at the same game, but they found us well prepared and the attack was stopped. We killed a number of their soldiers, and the following day, a sniper shot one of my sentries, I think perhaps a family member of one of the BiH soldiers who'd been shot. But that -- and I warned General -- Brigadier Barto [phoen], the commander of the 81st Division, that we would continue to resist and defend ourselves if we were further attacked. But even so, he thought it likely that there were those under his command that he would not be able to control and that they might well attack us again because they were desperate. He himself had -- I should add to that by saying that he himself had given orders that -- having received a directive, I believe from President Izetbegovic, that our move was not to be obstructed, but he did not feel confident that he could get everybody under his command to obey it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mention a meeting that General Mladic had with you and General Smith and at which he gave you guarantees that he would assist you with your withdrawal and you said that he kept his word. "Regardless of fierce Muslim attacks, whose aim was to block our movement, we were able to pull out of Gorazde and cross the Serbian territory without a single loss of life." Now, in relation to this let me ask you the following. When did this meeting between yourself, General Mladic, and General Smith take place?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Again, I'm afraid, off the top of my head, I can't remember the exact date. May I consult with the book, Your Honour, to verify the date if I can?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's just about the date, please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we perhaps --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if you would try to find it during the next break if it's that important. Meanwhile, answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was sometime I think in early August.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recall where the meeting took place, and apart from General Smith and General Mladic and yourself, was anyone else present?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: The meeting I think took place at Sokolac or somewhere near it. It was certainly on a ranch. I remember there were a lot of horses. Also the meeting really was between General Smith and General Mladic. I was invited to attend. Also present I remember Major Richard Wesley. Also there was another colonel called Popovic, not the same Popovic that I referred to earlier on, and I remember General Mladic saying to this officer: You will remain on the ground in the Serb municipality of Gorazde and you will act as the point of contact and you will make certain that the evacuation runs smoothly. The other person I remember being there was Brane Suka, who I can assure you exists. And, in fact, I remember meeting him in 1999, so he was still in the area then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could I ask some -- it's a bit unclear to me reading paragraph 30 when you're expressing that there was genuine concern about the safety of you and your troops or whether it's the assistance in withdrawing smoothly would also serve the interests of the Bosnian Serb army who then have no presence -- your presence would then be finished in the area. Could you tell us how you experienced this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the -- you're referring to the obstruction from the Bosnian side, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But also the assistance you got in order to overcome such obstruction because, in paragraph 30, we see that you said that General Mladic was true to his words that -- and that you were able to extract from Gorazde without loss of a single life.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, sir, there were two phases to the extraction on any one day. The first was to get out of the town of Gorazde as far as the confrontation line and across the confrontation line, which was territory controlled by the Bosnian army. So for the first part we were -- we -- there was the potential for a fight with them. And they had been obstructive, they had been told not to be obstructive. So we had to overcome that part. A relatively short distance from the town to -- of about 3 kilometres, corresponding with the old TEZ. Once across the confrontation line we were then into the territory controlled by the VRS, Bosnian Serb army, which was where General Mladic's authority ran. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- from there on we were in his hands, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you said: So for the first part we were -- there was the potential fact for a fight with them, "them" being the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With whom we'd had a fight three days before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is obstructing you leaving that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- territory.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly so, sir, exactly so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And my question was about -- I do see that you were assisted later by the Bosnian Serb army not to be bothered when you went through territory which was held by them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I'm seeking your interpretation of whether the primary concern was to get rid of you from that area or whether the primary concern was genuine concern about your safety or the two of them? Or how did you experience that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm -- sir, it's speculation on my part. But I think we were, by this stage, more trouble than we were worth to either side. And I think both of them just wanted us off their territory. The other enclaves had disappeared, they'd been captured, and we were -- we were now a historical accident, if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, I did hear in your answers that the Muslim forces might want to keep you there. So to say that your presence was not in the interest of neither party --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it depends at what level you're at on the Muslim side, sir. As far as the Bosnian government and the military command in the enclave was concerned, okay, we understand, leave. But lower down, at -- the troops on the ground, they -- they did not understand the bigger picture and were not -- and it was not explained to them. All they could see was the Brits were leaving and we're being left to stand up to the Serbs on our own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would just briefly go back to your observation. It is not our intention at all to invent --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Lukic please repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name you referred to. Therefore, perhaps you start with: It's not your intention at all to invent ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Brane Suka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Our assertion is that he had no direct relationship with General Mladic. As far as we were able to reveal, he spoke English; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: No, he did not speak English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was he a liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: That's what I was led to believe. He was not a regular soldier; he was a reservist. And he was still in the area in 1999, but he told me in 1999 that he was thinking of emigrating to Canada which is perhaps why you can't find him. Forgive me, I didn't mean to suggest that you were -- that we were trying to invent anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Concerning the correction that you made in paragraph 30, I can see that you often have to refer to your notes because you gave your statement in 1996. You would agree with me that your memory was much better in 1996 than it is today with regard to the events of 1995?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is an underlying suggestion, Mr. Lukic - I don't know whether you intended to convey that to the witness - you talked about consulting notes. Do you remember what -- when re-reading this, what made you decide that it was wrong that you were informed about NATO air-strikes, and that it was, rather, the shelling that you were informed about? Was it after you had consulted notes or what after 20 years made you decide that your statement is wrong and your testimony today is right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In preparation for this hearing, Your Honour, I re-read my diaries of the time and the published accounts of the battalion's tour which were drawn from the war diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the war diary predates your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does. It's contemporary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: According to the reports that we received from the Prosecution as proofing notes, you had not made this correction earlier. You did it for the first time today or, perhaps, we were not informed about any corrections you made during your proofing. We received two reports from the Prosecution and none of them contains this correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the proofing notes contain additional information coming from this witness. This particular clarification was made during the witness's Karadzic testimony, and on that basis there is no additional information and therefore it was not included in a proofing note sent yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore when Mr. Lukic said that the witness had not made the correction earlier, you say it's to be found in the Karadzic testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the perception of the Serbian side on the 25th of May, that is to say, during NATO strikes on Serbian positions, was that UNPROFOR forces and the Muslim forces were fighting side by side, that is to say, on the same side. During proofing you have been shown a document to that effect which says that in an order issued by the Drina Corps on the 25th of May, it is said that it is to be expected that the Muslim forces alongside UNPROFOR forces would continue to target the positions of the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I would agree with you that the perception could well be that, but perception is not necessarily truth or reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I found in a document the fact that vehicles confiscated from your units were repainted in the colours of Republika Srpska. They did not retain their original colours.

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Yes, I saw one of these vehicles myself painted in camouflage, and it had been modified by having a heavy-weapons turret mounted on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After a year, all the confiscated equipment was returned to your unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Yes, it -- yes, it was. Certainly the things like helmets, body armour, rifles were returned. I think it was some time later that the vehicles came back, but the three that were undamaged came back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could -- do you know what triggered this material to be returned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Your Honour, this was during the time that IFOR, the NATO Implementation Force, was in -- was deployed. Now, this was a force that was there on a very different mandate and it could enforce various matters, and it had the authority to inspect stores and weapons caches. And I think it was during one of their inspections that this equipment was found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it was not a spontaneous return to the former owners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not as far as I'm aware, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And this was after Dayton?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You showed us the map today which showed the deployment of your men in Republika Srpska, or rather, people who were imprisoned in Republika Srpska. Would you agree with me that prisoners of that sort cannot be kept in one place all the time, but rather have to be moved from one location to another?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: You're referring to the soldiers taken hostage on the -- on Sjenokos and the east bank?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are using the term "taken hostage" --

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Have your soldiers ever told you that they were told that they were prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: At least one told me that he was led to believe that he was a prisoner of war, and as far as I'm aware, they were treated as if they were prisoners of war and I have no issue with the way that they were treated. They were treated correctly throughout. That is not the point. They were entitled to the protection of peacekeepers and should not have been taken prisoner or hostage at all. And as to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- moving them around, I'm afraid that's neither here nor there. If they shouldn't have been taken, then whether they're moved or not is also neither here nor there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say "treated correctly," could I ask you whether you considered part of the correct treatment that they were put close to possible military targets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not. I was referring to their personal welfare, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were fed. They were given medical treatment. They were not threatened. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I do understand --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have not included that part of their treatment in your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, indeed, Your Honour, and thank you for prompting me. But that is -- and, of course, they were as -- because they were entitled to protection as peacekeepers, and indeed if they had been prisoners of war, they should not have been placed in harm's way deliberately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic. By the way, I see that we are at the time for a break. Could you tell us how much time you would still need.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that does not only depend on you but also on Mr. Jeremy. I don't know how much time Mr. Jeremy would still need, but I would like to ask him after you have told us how much time you would still need.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you know, I always have a lot, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the reason why I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe you should ask Mr. Jeremy first and then I cut my cross shorter as much as needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, as matters stand now and not knowing how much Mr. Lukic still has when he's going through his papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: As matters stand, Your Honours, five, max ten minutes, closer to five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll finish this witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if you would finish even -- if you would leave five more minutes, I could read a decision from the Chamber which the parties might be interested to know. Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could we release the next witness, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next witness can be released -- but I thought he was -- oh, yes, he was available. Yes. Then could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you announced two and a half hours, Mr. Lukic. You have used - and that's always net time - one hour and 54 minutes, which leaves a little bit over half an hour. So I would aim at finishing at 2.00. We take a break and we resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Forgive me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You asked me to check some dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I can give you all those dates now if that will be helpful because they will address Mr. Lukic's problem -- questions. The date of the meeting with Air Marshal Ratan, according to my information, in Beograd, was on the 23rd of July. The British government's announcement that we would leave Gorazde and not be replaced was the 18th of August. And the date that General Smith and General Mladic met at Borike which I was present was the 20th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, for these informations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have 65 ter 19790, that's a Prosecution number, could we please have that briefly in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit P2544, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is the document I do not need. I will try with another number. It's P1849, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we see a document here, a document of the Army of Republika Srpska of the Main Staff, dated the 27th of May, 1995. It is stated here that there was some intelligence to the effect that the NATO session was concluded on the 27th of May at around 1600 hours and that it was decided that massive NATO air-strikes against VRS positions and features would continue. On the ground, did you receive this information?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I've never seen that document before, so no, I did not receive that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I do apologise if I was not clear. Did you have information about the NATO session and that it was decided at that session held on the 27th of May to continue bombing Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: No, I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Today you said to us that members of your unit from the SAS provided information to NATO aircraft about targets. Was that the mandate of your unit, to provide information about targets to NATO aircraft?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: The mandate of my unit was to observe the TEZ and to deter attacks on the safe area. The mandate would not specify such things as you're talking about. These are procedures. They would -- they might be referred to in the rules of engagement. The rules of engagement for the Gorazde force were more robust than they were for UNPROFOR forces elsewhere, and they allowed indirect fires, such as aircraft, to be used in defence of the mission and in defence of the safe area. I provided a copy of the rules of engagement during my evidence in the Karadzic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the Serb side informed about that part of your mandate and did they know about that, namely, that members of your unit were guiding NATO aircraft?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Well, first of all, can I restate that it's -- that a procedure like that to employ a particular means is not -- would not be specified under the mandate. The mandate was issued by the United Nations. And as far as informing either side, no, I don't think I would have informed either side exactly what my capabilities were. But in any case, as I have already said, during my time in command in Gorazde no air-strikes were launched or directed by those tactical air control parties under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now take a look at P2481.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document was shown to you by my colleague, Mr. Jeremy. I would just like to ask you to take a look at the introductory part, where it says the president of Republika Srpska ordered, by way of his order, that on the 2nd of June, 1995, 120 members of UNPROFOR should be released. This document was signed by General --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, can we see the bottom of the page and the signature, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have the name typewritten here, the name of General Ratko Mladic. Would you agree that in this case it only has to do with conveying an order not actually issuing one?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: You mean that the president had given an instruction and that the General is therefore issuing a military order to carry out that instruction?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the supreme commander of the Army of Republika Srpska at the time was Mr. Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I do. I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So he issues orders, doesn't he? He can issue orders as the supreme commander. It wasn't an instruction. It was an order, as we can see from this document. [In English] "By the order."

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So would you now agree that it has to do with conveying an order rather than issuing it?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a question at this point in time. Mr. Riley, if you look at this -- the heading, it is said there: "Release of prisoners of war from UNPROFOR, order." Later we see that the prisoners should be released and handed over together with their personal equipment and weapons in the Pale sector to the MUP of the Republika Srpska, which will organise their transport to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Could you explain this procedure, handing over to the Ministry of Interior in order to transport them to Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, we can take issue with the term "prisoners of war," which they were not but that's how they're being described. I would -- in my professional opinion, they're being handed over to the -- the Ministry of Interior police who would then relieve the military of the responsibility for holding these hostages. And they would organise the transportation, and in the case of the British soldiers, I believe they went to Zvornik where they were met by the British ambassador. The Ministry of Interior police would have the authority and the means to move all these people across the various boundaries of the army corps, and it would, I would guess, just be a matter of making it more simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But would you consider that as a release? A release, a direct release would mean to set free so that they could return to their original place of -- where they have been before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There may be some linguistic issue here which I'm not aware of, but I would take this to mean these prisoners are to be released from the places of captivity where they are held into the -- into the custody or care of the Ministry of Interior police who will then take charge of them and transport them further on. I don't think here that they're being given their liberty; I think they're being released from close confinement, but that's not the same thing as regaining their liberty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And they wouldn't be able to continue fulfilling the task of UNPROFOR; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at this point, no. Because although it says that they will be handed over with their personal equipment and weapons, I think all that they had was their personal belongings. They were not robbed. And they had their clothes, but they did not have their weapons, body armour, helmets, and other military equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nor did they have any communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one additional question as well. Mr. Lukic asked you about whether this was issuing an order by General Mladic or whether it was just conveying an order. Now, the text reads, and I'm reading from the last line of page 1: "Pursuant to the order of the president of the Republika Srpska, I hereby order ..." Now, in normal military language, if you receive an order from your superior which needs to be implemented in the organisation, would you then say: I convey to you an order given by the president? Or would you -- or would the normal military structure require that you then pass on that order by issuing an order yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would incline myself to the latter. I would say that if you are given an order, you must accept the responsibility of carrying that order. Having accepted that responsibility, you then must issue the more detailed orders to all of your subordinates from your own authority which has come down to you from above.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would receive an illegal order, would you take responsibility by then ordering it further down the line to your subordinates? Would that make you responsible for the order --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you accept an illegal order and pass it on, then you are -- then you are, as an individual, culpable. Illegal orders should not be obeyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can't say: I just received this order --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I convey it to you, it's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everyone is responsible for the consequences of their actions, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And if something's illegal, it's illegal. The law is the law and the law is for everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, apparently a lot of attention was paid to the question whether the order was conveyed or whether an order was issued. Is this a semantic issue or is it something of substance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't see that it's a matter of substance. I think the president is giving an order or an instruction - call it what you will - to make this release. General Mladic is issuing a subsequent order which implements it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm getting close to the end now. Actually, first I'm going to ask you something. At that moment when NATO aircraft are bombing Serb positions, does UNPROFOR still maintain the peace in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: You're talking about the air-strikes around Pale in May?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Yes, it does because it was mandated by the United Nations, and I'm not aware, Mr. Lukic, of any higher authority in the world than that. And if the United Nations says that UNPROFOR is there to carry out a particular plan, then that should be the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view, in your view, was UNPROFOR impartial at that moment?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Impartiality does not mean that you have to treat both parties in a conflict, or all parties, in exactly the same way. You may treat them differently in order to make sure that your mandate is fulfilled. And that is in accordance with the UN's own definition of impartiality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D911, could we please take a look at that document now. This is an order of the commander of the Main Staff of UNPROFOR, General Smith. We'd be interested in number 4 at the very bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: According to General Smith, under (A), UNPROFOR no longer have a peacekeeping relationship with the VRS. It has lost the consent of one of the parties. And also, according to General Smith, under (B), UNPROFOR is very close to being an ally of the Bosnian government. It is very nearly no longer impartial. Would you agree with me that your view of the role and relationship of UNPROFOR does not tally with that of General Smith's?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: You asked me about what was going on at the time of the air-strikes. This document refers to the subsequent situation, after the bombing, after hostage taking, and so on. I would suggest that you are describing a changed situation, not the one you asked me about. May I see the second page of this so I can see the context in which those --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document has a few pages. We can take a look now. We can look at point (C) on the next page, where it says that UNPROFOR resorted to force in order to carry out its mandate. And then there was a possibility of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can no longer see the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have go back to page 1 in the English. (C) on the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You heard Judge Fluegge, can we go to page 1?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are -- it's on the screen now on the very bottom part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay, in English it is. I was watching B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's all on the screen. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I should proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. I just assisted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So since this is a document dated 29th of May, 1995, do you believe, then, that on that date this is applicable and that General Smith was right, that there was no peacekeeping relationship between them and the army of the Bosnian Serbs and that UNPROFOR is very close to becoming an ally of the Bosnian government?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Very close to but not having become, and in fact it never did, as far as I'm concerned, during my time there. I'd also like to draw your attention to the very first sentence. And there is General Smith telling us what this paper is about. First of all, he says it is to give us an idea about the debate that is going on, and the second is to direct our actions. So we should not confuse the two things. But he was right to say that in the aftermath of air-strikes and hostage taking, clearly consent on one side had broken down. But consent, in my experience, is not an absolute concept in peacekeeping operations. It is a relative, and one of the ways it is relative is through time. It can break down at times and it then can be re-established.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under item 4, General, we are nearing the end. I will not bother you any longer. We see here in the last sentence, before sub-item (a), it says UNPROFOR hold four BSA soldiers. According to you, are these soldiers hostages or prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: They were not held by me and I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were ready to say that UNPROFOR captives were hostages. What about the soldiers of the Serbian army? Were they hostages or were they prisoners of war? Was UNPROFOR entitled to take hostages or to take prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you'd like to tell me the circumstances in which they were taken and then I'll be able to answer you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that they were taken prisoner on Vrbanja Most in Sarajevo by UNPROFOR. At the time when the Bosnian Serb Army was taking prisoner members of UNPROFOR, at the same moment, UNPROFOR took the four BSA soldiers prisoner.

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: So what you're telling me is that the Bosnian Serb Army was carrying out a wholly improper action, possibly criminal, attacking peacekeeping troops in Sarajevo, during which those peacekeeping troops, in defending themselves, took four of their attackers?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Sorry. Just a moment. The French UNPROFOR members attacked a check-point of the Army of Republika Srpska and took these four soldiers prisoner.

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: That's not what you -- that's not what you said. You said this was during the time when the Bosnian Serb Army was taking hostages, taking prisoners, in your words.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] At the same time, but that what -- this is what happened, that French UNPROFOR members attacked one observation post of control point of Army of Republika Srpska and took four soldiers in their custody. I'm asking you to compare those two situations.

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I don't think there is any comparison. I have no means of verifying whether what you say, in fact, was what happened on the ground. I do recall that there was some serious fighting on that bridge and around it, according to reports that I saw, between the French UNPROFOR contingent and the VRS. And during -- and if during that exchange that's where those soldiers were taken, then I would say that the UNPROFOR troops, being as they were protected by the UN mandate, were protecting themselves as they were entitled to do so. Now, I don't know the specifics of exactly how those four soldiers were taken, so I can't comment on the modalities of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I think you -- you gave it an effort to explain to the witness what the situation was and asked him to make a comparison, whereas this witness appears here to tell us about what he personally observed and what he personally experienced. It not surprisingly ends into a discussion: Give me more details, tell me exactly what happened, et cetera. That should be dealt with by witnesses who have personal knowledge about the situation. Therefore, I think it's -- doesn't assist the Chamber to continue this feeding the witness with more information and then him asking for further information. So let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would just like to tender this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D911 receives number D390, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I'm looking at the clock --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will give up my intention to read the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have one short --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, you said five to ten minutes. Where are we?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Ten minutes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just have one more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question. Okay. We'll count them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, can you just tell us briefly, what happened to the Ukrainian members of UNPROFOR in Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: The Ukrainian members were -- their camp was attacked by the Bosnian army. They were -- they did not defend themselves. They were stripped of their weapons and equipment. I had then to take them into my care, and they were then removed at a later date by the Russian UNPROFOR contingent. I was very angry about this indeed, very angry, but by the time I became fully aware of the situation, I couldn't stop it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, for answering my questions. I have no further questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, any questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: General Riley, in cross-examination today at temporary transcript page 41, during a discussion of whether or not General Mladic ordered the BritBat camp in Gorazde to be shelled if there were further air-strikes, the following was put to you about Brane Suka, a man that you recall as a VRS liaison officer, and this is at transcript page 42, lines 13 to 14: "Trust me, I tried to find out who Brane Suka is. This man has no connection to General Mladic whatsoever." This was repeated again at temporary transcript page 65 today. Now, in response you stated that when you were called to a meeting with General Smith and General Mladic in August 1995, this man, Brane Suka, was present. In connection with that answer I'd like to show you a document, P345, and this is a -- this is the diary of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And specifically I'd like to see page 310 in the English and 314 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: General Riley, when this -- the English version is on the screen before you, I would like you to focus on the second entry halfway down the page. We see the location is Borike, dated the 22nd of August, 1995. The title of the meeting is: "Meeting with General Smith." We see is says: "Present: Smith, John, (Colonel)," and some other names. And we see it says: "Our side," it says, "Colonel Djurdjic, Indjic, Kusic, Krunic, Kosoric, Suka." And if we can go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Kusic was the brigade commander at Rogatica and I think that the meeting took place in his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: We also see Popovic, Furtula, and I, and interpreter Tijana. General Riley, is this the meeting that you attended in relation to the withdrawal of your battalion from Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: I believe it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And when --

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: And there is Suka present. And my clear recollection of that is that General Mladic knew him and addressed him as if he knew him. The -- I'm not quite sure why the -- there was an issue about Brane Suka. Brane Suka was -- was a thoroughly good man, a patriot as he saw it. He hated the war and would have done anything to see the situation resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to show the witness one final document, again in connection with Brane Suka. That's 65 ter 23892.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: General Riley, now that's on the screen we see it's a document from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, sector for security and intelligence, dated the 7th of May, 1995, addressed to the Drina Corps command, also addressed to the 5th Light Infantry Brigade command, and we see a reference to Captain Brane Suka personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we could also go to the second page in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I won't read it, but in the second paragraph again we see a reference to Brane Suka. And in the fifth -- the fourth paragraph we see a reference to: "Our liaison officer, Captain Suka, will condition the medical and social evacuation of release of captured Serbs in Gorazde ..." Does that help you refresh your recollection or corroborate your recollection about who this Captain Suka was?

utterances.speaker: JONATHON RILEY
utterances.text: Yes, and I recall the particular exchange and evacuation episode concerned. And I can only reiterate what I said earlier, that Brane Suka was based in the Serb municipality of Gorazde with Furtula's headquarters, but I was always led to understand that he was there to maintain liaison directly with General Mladic, which is what it seems that these documents are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender that document as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 23892 receives number P2547, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2547 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Riley.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, as the re-examination triggered any need for further questions? If Mr. Mladic - we are at the very end - wants to consult with you, of course you have an opportunity to -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Voice down, please. Mr. -- voice down, I said, and then I expect the volume to go down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you. Mr. Riley, this concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and/or by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn for the day and we will resume Monday, the 28th of October, 9.30 in the morning, Courtroom III. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 28th day of October, 2013, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.16 p.m.,
